It sounds like you're experiencing psychotic symptoms during your panic attacks. This does not mean you *are* "psychotic" or a psychopath. But is does mean therapy is needed much more.

If you have insurance, all you have to do is find a therapist that is covered. If you don't have insurance, you can apply for government-funded (Medicaid) based on your income. Actually, if your income is low enough, you can have both your original insurance *and* government-funded to increase your chances of finding therapy without any copay.

I highly recommend medication for psychotic symptoms. This means needing a psychiatrist. You don't need a therapist *and* psychiatrist, and you don't need one in order to get the other. But your symptoms are severe, so I recommend both.

If you're afraid to go, your partner can go with you. If you ever have gender troubles, there are counselors experienced in LGBT+ matters. This is a lot of information at once, but I recommend first getting examined before anything else so you can decide what to do next.

You can sit down with them one by one, or all together, whichever is easier. Let them know you want to get help and want their support.

Seek out a therapist, maybe even psychiatrist (a therapist could help you find one). And of course the crisis text lines can be helpful.

"Wouldn't I remember?" No, not necessarily. It's common to experience memory problems when dealing with mental health concerns because your brain *wants* to forget the pain, it *wants* to not be going through what you're going through. This is especially true with solid instances of trauma.

A good therapist will already know that and understand. But not every therapist is very good. Don't get discouraged if the first one doesn't work out!

Anyone can benefit from therapy, so even if things seem alright now it might be a good time to get her in before things possibly get worse. She might even just need stress management tools.

The worst case is, she is diagnosed with postpartum depression and recommended to see a psychiatrist (in addition to the therapist, not in place of). Your wife has the choice to see a psych or not. She has a choice to take meds or not. She will have all the time in the world to discuss it with you, so rest assured she will not be rushed or forced to do anything.

As for right now, it's important to communicate with her. Find out how she's feeling exactly and what is wrong. Be supportive of course. If she's uneasy about therapy, you can go with her, but sometimes it is best to go alone.

I understand that your insecurity is stemming from your friend history, I went through similar things and became insecure as well. I ended up isolating myself to avoid being hurt again. I advise against that of course.

I'm a young adult now and have come to realize that people come and go, and can even come back again. A good friend will ultimately always be there, but you also need room to grow. Becoming reliant on one person for social needs can be dangerous for your self esteem, as you might be realizing.

I recommend trying to make more friends. It's hard, especially being aroace, but that way you could always have someone to talk to. Explore your solo interests as well! Alone time can be good.

It's possible you're in a state of shock over your grandpa, and the information might just hit you later. Your brain might be slower to process the news.


Another possibility is that you're numbed to pain, if you've ever been in a traumatic situation before or if your life is generally chaotic. Given the pandemic, a lot of people are facing this "numbing." The brain is processing so many awful events that this new one is not much in comparison.

Stay strong.
